passages.t: An old man's farewell: ‘hold fast to the LORD’
passages.happening:
A long time has passed since the wars. Israel has had rest, and Joshua is old. He calls together the elders, leaders, judges and officers of all Israel (verses 1-2).

“I am old and well along in years,” he says. He asks them to remember what they have seen with their own eyes, ‘because it was the LORD your God who fought for you’ (verse 3). The land has been shared out among the tribes, the nations already defeated and the nations that remain. The LORD will drive out those that are left, as he promised (verses 4-5).

Then comes the charge. “Be very strong, then, so that you can keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, not turning aside from it to the right or to the left” (verse 6). They are not to mix with the nations that remain, or call on the names of their gods, or swear by them, or serve them, or bow down to them (verse 7).

“Instead, you shall hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The Bible has several great farewell speeches: Moses at the end of Deuteronomy, Samuel when he steps down, David on his deathbed. This is Joshua's. A leader near the end of his life gathers the people and says what he most wants them to remember.

He begins with what God has done. Joshua commanded the army in every battle of this book, and he does not mention himself. He says that it was the LORD who fought.

Then he gives the leaders the words God gave him at the start. In chapter 1 God told Joshua to be strong, to keep the law of Moses, and to turn from it neither to the right nor to the left. Joshua has lived by that. Now he hands it on in nearly the same words. He has no new teaching to leave them. He leaves them the one he received.

The situation he describes is the one the book has been honest about since chapter 13. The great kings are broken, but many peoples still live in the land, and they have their own gods. The danger now is not on a battlefield. It is next door.

His warning about their gods climbs by steps. Do not call on their names. Do not swear by them. Do not serve them. Do not bow to them. In the ancient world, to swear an oath by a god was to treat that god as real and as the guard of one's word. Joshua draws the line well back from open worship. Faithfulness is lost in small acts of respect long before anyone bows down.

Against all that he sets one phrase, ‘hold fast’. The Hebrew word means to cling. It is the word used in Genesis for a man holding fast to his wife. Joshua is not asking only for correct belief. He is asking for attachment.

And he adds a word of honest praise: ‘as you have done to this day’. This generation has been faithful, and he says so.
passages.later:
God's charge to Joshua at the beginning of the book used the same words: “Do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may prosper wherever you go” (Joshua 1:7).

Moses had asked for the same clinging: “You are to fear the LORD your God and serve Him. Hold fast to Him and take your oaths in His name” (Deuteronomy 10:20).

The letter to the Hebrews gives the reason anyone can hold on: “Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful” (Hebrews 10:23).
passages.asks: Joshua had no new message at the end. He passed on the words he had been given at the start. Ask what you were taught early that you most want to hand on, and to whom. Then think about his steps: naming, swearing by, serving, bowing down. Ask what in the world around you has begun to earn small acts of respect from you that belong to God.

passages.t: ‘Watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD’
passages.happening:
Joshua reminds them of what God has done so far. “The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations before you, and to this day no one can stand against you. One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised” (verses 9-10).

From that he draws his plea. “Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God” (verse 11).

Then he warns. If they turn away and cling to the nations that remain, and marry among them and join with them, ‘know for sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you’ (verse 13). The peoples they have embraced will become ‘a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes’, until Israel itself perishes from the good land God has given (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The center of the speech is verse 11, and it is about love. Joshua has spoken of law, strength and obedience. At the heart of it he says: take care that you love the LORD. It is the language of Deuteronomy, where the first of all commands is to love God with heart and soul and strength. Love of this kind is loyalty first, shown in what a person does. It is also more than duty.

‘Watch yourselves’ admits something. Love for God can fade without anyone deciding that it should. It needs guarding.

The same word comes back with a different object. In verse 8 Israel is to hold fast to the LORD. In verse 12 the danger is that Israel will ‘cling’ to the nations. It is one Hebrew verb. Joshua's point is that a people will cling to something. The only question is to what.

The warning about marriage needs to be read with care, and the hard question below takes it up. In brief, the reason given is worship and not race.

The pictures at the end are taken from hunting and from pain. A snare is a bird trap. It looks like nothing until it closes. Joshua does not say that the nations will attack Israel. He says they will catch it. What seems a harmless friendship with their gods will, in time, cost Israel the land.

That is the edge of the whole speech. The land was a gift, and the gift could be lost. The same God who drove out other nations for their wickedness would not keep Israel there whatever it did. The book of Judges begins to tell that story.
passages.later:
Moses had given the reason for the warning about marriage: “Do not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).

The book of Judges reports God's own verdict a generation later, in Joshua's very words: “So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you; they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you” (Judges 2:3).

The Old Testament also tells of a woman from one of the nations who clung to the right thing. Ruth the Moabite said to her Israelite mother-in-law, ‘your people will be my people, and your God will be my God’ (Ruth 1:16).
passages.hard:
Joshua warns Israel not to marry among the nations. Is that not prejudice against other peoples?

Read by itself it can sound like it. But the reason given, here and in Deuteronomy 7, is about worship. Such marriages, Moses says, will turn Israel's children ‘to serve other gods’. In the ancient world a marriage joined two families and usually brought the gods of both into one house.

The Old Testament itself shows that the concern was faith and not blood. Rahab, a Canaanite of Jericho, and Ruth, a woman of Moab, both turned to Israel's God. Both were welcomed, both married Israelites, and both stand in the family line of King David and of Jesus.

Some readers still find the command hard, and see it as tied to Israel's particular moment, a new nation among many gods. Most Christian readers find its lasting point in Paul's counsel that a believer who marries should marry ‘in the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 7:39). They do not find in it any rule about race or nation.

Passages like this have been misused to forbid marriages between people of different races or peoples and to rank one people above another. That is a false use of it. The passage supports no contempt for any people, and it lays down no rule about the color or origin of the person anyone marries.
passages.asks: Joshua said to watch yourselves, that you love the LORD. Ask whether your love for God is something you are guarding, or something you assume will look after itself. Ask what you are clinging to. And ask what in your life looks harmless and is slowly closing, like a snare.

passages.happening:
Joshua speaks of his own death. “Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed. Everything was fulfilled for you; not one promise has failed” (verse 14).

Then he turns the same truth around. “But just as every good thing the LORD your God promised you has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring upon you the calamity He has threatened, until He has destroyed you from this good land He has given you” (verse 15).

He names what would bring it. If they break the covenant of the LORD their God and go and serve other gods and bow down to them, his anger will burn against them, and they ‘will quickly perish from this good land He has given you’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘The way of all the earth’ is a plain way to speak of dying. It is the road every person takes. Joshua does not dress it up. He is old, he is going to die, and he says so to their faces.

A dying man's words carry weight, and Joshua spends his on one claim. God has kept every good promise. He says it over and over in one verse, and he calls his hearers as witnesses: ‘you know with all your heart and soul’. The Hebrew says that not one word has ‘fallen’, as if a promise that failed would drop to the ground. None did.

Then comes the turn that makes this speech hard to hear. God's faithfulness is not only comfort. If he keeps his word about good, he will keep his word about harm. The reliability that gave Israel the land is the same reliability that will take it away if Israel abandons him. Joshua will not let them have a God who keeps only the pleasant half of what he says.

The phrase ‘this good land’ comes three times in the last four verses of the chapter. Each time it is called a land that God has given. Joshua wants them to feel what they stand to lose. It is good, it was given, and it is not theirs beyond recall.

The covenant he speaks of is the agreement God made with Israel at Mount Sinai, with its promises and its duties. To ‘transgress’ it is, in Hebrew, to cross over its boundary.

These warnings were spoken to a nation about its life in a land under a covenant. They are not a rule for reading any one person's troubles, and they are no ground for anyone to explain the later sufferings of the Jewish people as God's punishment. That use of such texts is false and has done great harm.
passages.later:
King David used Joshua's phrase when his own time came: “I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man” (1 Kings 2:2).

Paul says where the promises of God stand now: “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

And the prophets, who lived to see Joshua's warning come true, also saw beyond it. Through Jeremiah God said, “I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31).
passages.asks: Joshua used his last strength to say that God had kept every promise. Ask what you would want to say at the end, and whether you could say that. Then face the other half. Ask whether you trust a God who means everything he says, or have quietly kept only the comforting parts. And ask what you have been given that you are treating as if it could never be lost.
